(HIGH COURT OF ASSAM, NAGALAND, MIZORAM AND ARUNACHAL PRADESH)

BEFORE
HONOURABLE MRS. JUSTICE MARLI VANKUNG
ORDER
Date : 30.05.2023
Heard Mr. C. Lalfakzuala, learned counsel for the applicant/appellant, who has
filed this application under Section 389(1) Cr.P.C. for suspension of the sentence
imposed upon the applicant/appellant by the learned Judge, Special Court, Prevention
of Corruption Act, Aizawl in SR (PCA) No. 1/2020 vide Sentence Order dated
20.03.2023, wherein the applicant/appellant was sentenced under Section 420 r/w
Section 120B IPC to undergo 5 years imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 60 lakhs, i.d.
another imprisonment of 30 years, he was also sentenced under Section 477 A r/w
120B IPC to undergo 5 years imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 60 lakhs, i.d. another
imprisonment of 30 years and sentenced under Section 13(2) r/w Section 13(1)(c) &
(d) of PC Act, 1988 r/w Section 120B IPC to undergo 5 years imprisonment with a fine
of Rs. 60 lakhs, i.d. imprisonment for a term of 30 years. The terms of imprisonment
shall run concurrently except for the fine imposed.
The learned counsel for the applicant/appellant has prayed for the release of
the applicant/appellant on bail pending disposal of the connected appeal, which is
registered as Criminal Appeal No. 21/2023, mentioning that there are sufficient
grounds in which the conviction against the applicant/appellant is likely to be set aside
since the applicant/appellant was convicted mainly on the deposition of the two
prosecution witnesses, who had deposed before the Court that they had prepared
Page No.# 3/4
excessive bills on the verbal direction of the instant applicant/appellant. That the
applicant/appellant did not give such direction as alleged and the innocence of the
applicant/appellant can be brought out during the consideration of the Criminal Appeal
No. 21/2023. He further submits that the applicant/appellant is also having serious
medical ailments since he has had an implantation of a pace maker and he had to
take voluntary retirement due to his medical condition during the year, 2019. The
medical certificates showing the medical condition of the applicant/appellant have
been duly annexed along with the instant I.A.(Crl.) No. 29/2023. That the
applicant/appellant is now a senior citizen aged 63 years of age. Being a permanent
resident of Bawngkawn Brigade, there is no likelihood of him absconding during the
pendency of the Crl.A. No. 21/2023. That since he has already left his service on
voluntary retirement, there is no chance of him exerting any influence during the
pendency of the Crl.A. No. 21/2023. Further, since there are as many as 46
prosecution witnesses which were examined by the learned Trial Court, the
preparation of the paper book for the appeal is likely to take some time.
For the above reasons, he has prayed for the suspension of the sentence and
the release of the applicant/appellant on bail during the pendency of the Crl.A. No.
21/2023. The learned counsel for the applicant/appellant has relied on the judgments
of the Coordinate Bench in Dr. N. Palai Vs. CBI (Imphal) Case No. I.A.(Crl.) No.
32/2023 dated 29.05.2023, Linked Case Criminal Appeal No. 26/2023, Liansanga Vs.
State of Mizoram Case No. I.A.(Crl.) No. 26/2022, Linked Case No. Crl.A. No. 28/2022
and the decision of the Apex Court in Kali Ram Vs. State of Himachal Pradesh,
reported in 1973 2 SCC 808, which is regarding the silence of the witnesses who were
aware of the commission of an offence.
Mrs. Linda L. Fambawl, learned Additional Public Prosecutor, on the other hand
has strongly objected, mentioning that the applicant/appellant has been convicted for
Page No.# 4/4
economic offences committed by him wherein the misappropriated amount is a huge
amount of Rs. 1,73,48,365.00/- and that releasing him on bail at this stage would be
sending a wrong message to the society at large. That the evidence adduced in the
Trial Court clearly points out to the guilt of the applicant/appellant and the conviction
order of the learned Trial Court is most likely to be upheld in the Crl.A. No. 21/2023.
Having heard the submissions made by the learned counsels for both the
parties, this Court finds that the applicant/appellant is now aged 63 years and is
genuinely suffering from a serious ailments, he had to take voluntary retirement due
to his medical condition. It is also seen that LCR called for is not received till date by
his Registry and paper book is yet to be prepared. Therefore, considerable time may
be taken before the Crl.A. No. 21/2023 can be heard on merits by the Court.
In view of the above and also considering the fact that since the
applicant/appellant is no longer in service, there is a bleak chance of him being able to
exert any influence during the pendency of the Crl.A. No. 21/2023, this Court find it fit
to suspend the sentence order of the learned Special Court dated 20.03.2023 and
release the applicant/appellant on bail with a bail bond of Rs. 50,000/- and with two
surety of the like amount, who shall be to the satisfaction of the Special Judge, PC
Act, Aizawl, Mizoram.
I.A.(Crl.) No. 29/2023 accordingly stands allowed and disposed.
JUDGE

judgments.case_name: Bail Appln./9/2023 of Lalduhsaka Vs State of Mizoram
judgments.text:
Page No.# 1/5
GAHC030001472023
THE GAUHATI HIGH COURT
(HIGH COURT OF ASSAM, NAGALAND, MIZORAM AND ARUNACHAL PRADESH)
Case No. : Bail Appln./9/2023
Lalduhsaka
S/o Lalrosanga, Chanmari West, Aizawl
VERSUS
State of Mizoram
Mizoram
Advocate for the Petitioner : Mr. Johny L Tochhawng
Advocate for the Respondent : Mrs. Linda L Fambawl
BEFORE
HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE NELSON SAILO
ORDER
21.04.2023
Heard Mr. Johny L. Tochhawng, learned counsel for the applicant who submits
that the applicant by filing this application under Section 439 of the CrPC prays for
grant of bail.
2. The learned counsel submits that the petitioner was arrested on 02.12.2022 at
around 10:00 pm by the Excise & Narcotics personnel for alleged possession of 12
grams of suspected heroin which were recovered from a nearby bush in Chanmari
West, Aizawl. The recovered substance was sent for forensic examination and the
Page No.# 2/5
same is found to be heroin with purity of 81% w/w.
3. Pursuant to the investigation conducted by the Excise & Narcotics personnel,
chargesheet was filed on 01.02.2023. While framing the charge, the applicant pleaded
not guilty and accordingly the matter is proceeded with for regular trial.
4. The learned counsel for the applicant submits that the applicant is innocent and he
is the sole breadwinner of the family. He submits that the applicant has three children,
aged 7 years, 4 years and 9 months and they are in constant need of medical
treatment. To substantiate the submission, the learned counsel has drawn the
attention of this Court to the medical documents annexed in the application as
annexures 11, 12 and 13. The learned counsel submits that if the applicants is
released on bail, the applicant undertakes to abide by any condition imposed by the
Court and he will extend full cooperation with the trial proceedings and will not jump
bail. In support of his submission, the learned counsel has relied upon the following
authorities:-
(i) Kheirun Bibi Vs. State of Manipur, (1994) 1 GLR 295.
(ii) Satender Kumar Antil Vs. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another,
(2022) 10 SCC 51.
5. Ms. Mary L. Khiangte, learned Addl. Public Prosecutor on the other hand submits
that the facts involved in the authorities relied upon by the learned counsel for the
applicants are different and cannot be applied to the instant case. She submits that in
Satender Kumar Antil (Supra), the observation and direction passed by the Apex Court
was regarding a situation before charge sheet is filed and trial begins. In the instant
case, the charge sheet has already been filed and the trial has begun. Similarly, in the
case of Kheirun Bibi (Supra), the applicant in that case was a person who was aged 50
years. Therefore, it was the considered view of the Court that there was no chance for
the person to commit similar offence and to jump bail if release. The same not being
the case in the present application, the bail application may be rejected.
Page No.# 3/5
6. I have heard the submissions made by the learned counsels for the rival parties and
I have perused the materials available on record.
7. The allegation against the applicant is that he has been found to be possessed 12
grams of suspected heroin. The same was sent for forensic examination and the same
tested to be heroin with purity of 81% w/w. The charge framed against the applicant
is under Section 21 (b) of the ND&PS Act and if convicted the punishment provided
Rigorous Imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and with fine and
which may extend to Rs. 100,000/-.
8. It is seen that during the pendency of the investigation, the applicant filed three
bail applications i.e. Bail Application No. 1513/2022, Bail Application No. 144/2023 and
Bail Application No. 156/2023 before the learned Trial Court. The first Bail Application
was rejected vide Order dated 14.12.2022 since there was ongoing investigation and
objection from the prosecution was advanced that the applicant may temper with the
evidence or abscond or even commit a similar offence if bail was granted. The bail
application was therefore rejected. Thereafter, in the second bail application, the
learned Trial Court considering the fact that the mandatory period of 60 days had not
expired, the learned Trial Court rejected the bail application vide Order dated
31.01.2023. In the third bail application, the learned Trial Court in view of the fact that
charge sheet was filed within a period of 60 days of the applicant being in custody
held that the applicant was not entitled to default bail under Section 167 of the CrPC.
As such, the bail application was again rejected.
9. By presenting the instant bail application before this Court, the learned counsel for
the applicant has projected the case of the applicant by submitting that the applicant
is the sole breadwinner of the family having three minor children who are unwell and
are solely dependent on the earning of the applicant. The learned counsel for the
applicant has also drawn the attention of this Court to the certificate given by the
Local Council of Chanmari West which states that the family members of the applicant
Page No.# 4/5
are not able to fend for themselves and it is the Local Council of the public of the
locality who are extending help to the family of the applicant. This factor alone
ordinarily may not be the ground for grant of bail but the fact remains that after the
filing of the chargesheet on 03.02.2023, charge was framed against the applicant and
to which he pleaded not guilty. Thereafter, the learned Trial Court has proceeded with
the Trial by asking the prosecution to link their evidence. It is submitted at the bar
that prosecution witness No. 1, who is the seizing officer has been summoned to give
her evidence by fixing 10.03.2023 for her appearance. However, PW1 failed to appear
on that date and therefore, another date i.e. 06.04.2023 was fixed for PW1 evidence.
Even on 06.04.2023, PW1 failed to appear and therefore, another date i.e. 03.05.2023
has been fixed for PW1 evidence. From the charge sheet produced by the learned
counsel for the applicant, it is seen that there are as many as 8 prosecution witnesses,
which includes two independent witnesses. The applicant admittedly has been in
custody since his arrest on 02.12.2022 and it is not known as to when the evidence of
the prosecution witnesses can be completed and the entire trial be concluded.
Therefore, upon considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the
considered view that the applicant should be enlarged on bail pending conclusion of
the trial.
10. In the result, the applicant is directed to be released on bail upon furnishing of bail
bond of Rs. 50,000/- with one surety of the like amount with the satisfaction of the
learned Trial Judge. The surety produced by the applicant should be certified by the
Local Council Chairman of Chanmari West, as a person who is a permanent resident of
the said locality.
11. The bail is granted to the applicant with the further condition that the applicant
shall not indulge himself in committing a similar offence and he shall appear before
the learned Trial Court as and when he is summoned.
12. With the above observations and directions, the bail application stands disposed
Page No.# 5/5
of.
JUDGE
Comparing Assistant

BEFORE
HONOURABLE MRS. JUSTICE MARLI VANKUNG
ORDER
Date : 29-03-2023
Heard Mr. C. Lalramzauva, learned Senior counsel for the petitioner.
This is an appeal filed under Section 27 of the PC Act, 1988 r/w Section 374
Cr.P.C against the impugned Judgment & Order dated 07.02.2023 along with the
sentence order dated 08.02.2023 passed by the Special Judge, Aizawl, Mizoram in SR
(PCA) No. 4/2012 (Ref: CBI, ACB, Imphal Case No. RC 6 (A) 2010-IMPH), convicting
the appellant under Section 420 r/w Section 120B IPC and sentenced to undergo 1
year imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 10 lakhs i.d., another imprisonment of 5 years
and under Section 467/468/471 r/w Section 120B IPC sentencing him to undergo 1
year imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 10 lakhs i.d., another imprisonment of 5 years,
where the sentences are to run concurrently except for the fine imposed.
The learned Senior counsel for the petitioner submits that there are sufficient
grounds for setting aside the judgment and order of the learned Special Judge, PC
Act, the main ground is due to the fact that the accused No. 1 and accused No. 9 have
been acquitted by the learned Special Court, wherein it can be clearly seen from the
examination of the petitioner under Section 313 Cr.P.C that the allegations made
against him arises from the action/steps that was taken by the accused No. 1 and
accused No. 9. Therefore, on their acquittal, there are now no grounds for the
conviction of the petitioner under the aforesaid sections.
On hearing the learned Senior counsel for the petitioner, this Court finds that a
prima facie grounds have been made out for filing an appeal against the Judgment &
Order dated 07.02.2023 along with the sentence order dated 08.02.2023 passed by
the Special Judge, Aizawl, Mizoram in SR (PCA) No. 4/2012 (Ref) CBI, ACB, Imphal
Page No.# 3/3
Case No. RC 6 (A 210-IMPH)
In view of the above, the appeal is admitted.
LCR is to be called for.
Issue notice upon the respondents through registered post with A/D within 3
days returnable by four weeks.
The petitioner is to take necessary steps.
List this matter after 4 (four) weeks.
JUDGE

judgments.case_name: Crl.A./6/2022 of Lalthakima Vs State of Mizoram
judgments.text:
Page No.# 1/30
GAHC030002012022
THE GAUHATI HIGH COURT
(HIGH COURT OF ASSAM, NAGALAND, MIZORAM AND ARUNACHAL PRADESH)
Case No. : Crl.A./6/2022
Lalthakima
S/o T. Chhunga
R/o Khawzawl Vengthar, Champhai, Mizoram
VERSUS
State of Mizoram
Aizawl, Mizoram
Advocate for the Petitioner : Mr. Lalpianfela Chawngthu
Advocate for the Respondent : Mrs. Linda L Fambawl, PP/Addl.PP, Mizoram
J & O (CAV)
UDGMENT RDER
[Soumitra Saikia, J.]
This criminal appeal arises out of the Judgment and Order dated
15.12.2021 passed by the learned Special Judge, NDPS Act, Champhai in SC
Regn. No. 299/2019 arising out of Crl. Tr. No. 1702/2019.
2. The appeal was admitted on 20.05.2022 and LCR was called for. After
receipt of the LCR, paper-book was prepared and served to the respective
counsel. The matter has thereafter been listed before this Court and taken up
for disposal in the presence of counsel representing both the parties.
Page No.# 2/30
3. The prosecution case as unfolded from the materials available on
record, is that on 15.08.2019 the informant one SI Zirthanga Pachuau, Sector
Officer, CID(SB), Champhai, lodged an FIR stating that on 15.08.2019 at about
3.30 PM a joint operation was conducted by CID(SB) led by Addl.
Superintendent Police, CID (SB)-Champhai, Champhai and DEF staff led by
th
SDPO Champhai and 8 Assam Rifles conducted random checking at
Zokhawthar Road near Hringlangtlang Junction (between Mualkawi and Melbuk
rd
Village) for the peaceful celebration of 73 India Independence Day, 2019. One
Maxi Cab bearing Registration No. MZ-02A-4009 driven by Malsawmdawngliana
(27), S/o: C. Dinthanga of Bawngkawan Aizawl coming from Zokhawthar side
was stopped on suspicious ground and upon thorough checking of the said
vehicle, the search party recovered from the said vehicle 30 (thirty) soap cases
of brown powder weighing 378.7 grams suspected to be Heroin worth Rs. 15
Lakhs approximately in the local market. The said contraband items was seized
from the joint possession of the driver Malsawmdawngliana (27) S/o: C.
Dinthanga of Bawngkawn Aizawl and the second driver Lalthakima (41) S/o: T.
Chhuma of Khawzawl Vengthar, namely, the appellant herein.
4. Pursuant to the investigations being carried out, charge-sheet was
submitted and charges under one head were framed against both the accused
persons including the appellant under Sections 21(c)/25/29 of the NDPS Act.
The accused persons pleaded not guilty. As such, the matter went for trial.
5. The prosecution had examined 5 (five) witnesses but the defence did not
present any witness. The Trial Court on the basis of the evidences adduced by
the prosecution had held that the prosecution had succeeded in bringing home
the charge against the accused persons under Sections 21(c)/25/29 of the NDPS
Act, 1985. The Trial Court therefore convicted the accused persons for
Page No.# 3/30
possession of 378.7 grams of heroin under Sections 21(c)/25/29 NDPS Act. The
Trial Court vide order dated 16.12.2021 sentenced the accused persons to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment for 12 (twelve) years each and to pay a fine of
Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees twenty thousand) each. In default of payment of the
fine, it was directed that they shall further undergo Simple Imprisonment for 2
(two) months each. It was further directed that the period of detention already
undergone by the accused persons in connection with this case shall be set off
against the sentence imposed.
6. Being aggrieved by the impugned Judgment dated 16.12.2021 passed by
the Special Judge, NDPS Act, Champhai, Judicial District, Champhai, the present
criminal appeal has been preferred on behalf of the accused No. 2 namely,
Lalthakima @ Thatea. We have been informed that no appeal has been
preferred by the accused No. 1.
7. P.W-1, Zirthanga Pachuau had identified the accused in the Court. He
deposed that on 15.08.2019, a police team under his command and under the
aegis of Addl. Superintendent of Police, namely Pu Laldingngheta, CID (SB)
performed random checking of vehicles plying on national highway between
Champhai and Zokhawthar particularly at a place called Hringlangtlang pend to
check infiltration and influx of anti-social in the event of peaceful celebration of
Independence day and also to deal with smuggling of contraband substances.
During the random checking of vehicles at around 3.30 P.M. Maxi Cab Sumo
bearing registration No. MZ02A-4009 which was coming from Zokhawthar was
stopped by the police party. Inside the vehicle only driver and another person
was seen. No other passengers or any luggage was found inside the vehicle.
The sumo looked empty. He gave signals to stop them but the driver was
looking nervous and uncomfortable and he therefore, strongly suspected that
Page No.# 4/30
something was wrong. P.W.1 requested the driver to switch off the car engine
and open the bonnet cover of the vehicle. The driver replied that there was a
mechanical problem and it was not possible to open the bonnet and further
stated that due to the mechanical problem they were coming to repair the
same. Upon being requested by the P.W.1 to show him how it was opened, the
driver of the vehicle opened the bonnet and from there one carton box placed
just close to the engine block was recovered. The P.W.1 thereafter instructed his
team to request civilian witnesses from nearby localities particularly office
bearers of YMA to be present before opening of the carton/box. The driver
identified himself as Malsawmdawngliana and his friend as identified as
Lalthakima as the second driver.
7.1 P.W.-1 has further deposed that when the civilian witnesses arrived, the
carton/box was opened and 30 (thrity) numbers of soap cases of different
colours were found. All of them contained substances suspected to be
Heroin. After opening the carton/box and finding the suspected heroin, he
immediately informed the matter to his Addl. Superintendent of Police by
phone. Thereafter, in the presence of the Addl. S.P. and one Army Officer who
th
was the Post Commander of 8 Assam Rifles from Zokhawthar, the seizure of
the contraband substances was made by P.W.1. The contraband substances
were weighed and it was found that it was altogether 378.7 grams. After
weighing the contraband, the plastic containers were re-packed/ re-sealed in
the presence of civilian witnesses and the team members. The P.W.-1 deposed
that no body search was conducted but he still prepared Grounds of Belief so
that the formalities were followed neatly. The P.W-1 deposed that he had
obtained authorization from Officer-in-Charge, Champhai Police Station prior to
his team setting out for the operation of random checking, despite the fact that
Page No.# 5/30
he was Sub-Inspector of Police duly authorized under the Act to conduct such
exercise of seizure etc. During the process of seizure of the contraband
substances, the Addl. S.P., CID (SB), SDPO, Champhai and Army Post
Commander were present along with civilian witnesses, Mr. Lalchhuanliana and
Mr. Lalrintluanga, leaders of YMA from Mualkawi village.
7.2 It was further deposed that statements of the witnesses were recorded
at the P.O and a seizure memo in respect of the heroin and the Maxi Cab Sumo
was prepared.
7.3 During his Cross Examination, P.W.-1 has deposed that he seized the
heroin and the maxi cab sumo with its ignition key. He deposed that he was not
aware of the owner of the maxi cab sumo nor does he know about the previous
criminal records of the two accused persons. He deposed that he was not
concerned with the entries made by the case I.O in the charge-sheet regarding
the particulars entered in respect of accused Lalthakima. He deposed that in his
FIR, he did not mention the name of owner of the maxi cab sumo. He deposed
that he does not know if the said sumo was produced before the Court or not
and that it is a fact that nothing was recovered from the sitting compartment of
passengers. He deposed that the heroin were seized from the sumo after
around 10 to 20 minutes of the apprehension of the accused the civilian
witnesses arrived. He deposed that the civilian witnesses were from the nearby
locality. The recovery, seizure, repacking etc were done in the presence of
civilian witnesses. He deposed that two accused persons neither claimed nor
denied ownership of the seized heroin. He deposed that the seized heroin were
more or less brown in colour.
8. P.W.-2, C. Lalchhuanliana, an independent witness identified the two
accused persons in Court. P.W-2 deposed that on 15.08.2019 at about 3.30 PM,
Page No.# 6/30
Champhai Police CID requested him to associate him with them at
Hringlangtkang Peng (national highway of Champhai to Zokhawthar) in
connection with the present case. He deposed that the police team in
collaboration with the Assam Rifles Personnel recovered a carton box/parcel
from inside the bonnet cover of maxi cab sumo bearing registration No. MZ 02A
4009 driven by Malsawmdawngliana S/O C Dinthanga R/O Bawngkawn, Aizawl
along with his friend Lalthakima S/O T Chhuma. The police recovered 30 plastic
soap cases from inside the carton box weighing 378.7 grams. He signed on the
seizure memo and he saw the police weighing the seized substances, repacking
and resealing it. P.W-2 identified his signature as Ext. P-3 (b).
8.1 In his cross-examination of P.W.-2 deposed that when he reached the
place of occurrence it might have been around 3.45 PM. He deposed that he
could not say for sure if two accused persons were inside the vehicle or outside
when he reached the place of occurrence. When he reached the place of
occurrence, he was not told that the police team was about to search the
vehicle. The PW-2 deposed that he did not remember the colour of the parcel.
Colours of the soap cases are “eng uk, sen uk, hring, eng etc.” which translated
to the Mizo language means “Dark yellow”, Dark Red”, “Green”, “Yellow”
respectively. Colour of the heroin was “a var lam deuh” which translated to Mizo
means “Probably it might be white”. He deposed that the two accused persons
never claimed ownership of the seized articles and that he did not know the
owner of the vehicle. The two accused persons also never claimed ownership of
the vehicle and the seized articles were also never recovered from the direct
possession of the accused. P.W.-2 further deposed that his statement, which was
submitted to the Court, was wrongly recorded by the SI Zirthanga Pachuau and
that the name of the two accused were not written in the parcel where the
Page No.# 7/30
seized articles were kept. He admitted that he put his signature on two pieces of
paper and denied the suggestion that he had deposed falsely.
9. P.W-3 was the Vice President of Mualkawi Branch of YMA at the
relevant time of the incident. On the date of occurrence, at around 3.30 PM, he
was requested by Champhai Police to associate himself with the present case.
He deposed that the police was undertaking an operation conducting checking
of vehicles on the national Highway between Champhai- Zokhawthar at a place
called Hringlangtlang Peng. P.W. -3 deposed that the team comprised of Assam
Rifles and CID Champhai personnel. P.W-3 deposed that the parcel/the carton
was recovered from the bonnet cover close to the engine block and the box was
not opened before his arrival. Upon the box being opened about 30 plastic soap
cases all containing substances suspected to be heroin were recovered. Weight
measured was found to be 378.7 grams and he put his signature on the seizure
memo as a seizure witness. He identified Exhibit P 3(c) as his signature.
9.1 In his cross-examination, the P.W-3 deposed that police came to P.W-3
and picked him up from his residence. He was never disclosed about the owner
of the vehicle by the police. His President informed him that he will have to go
to the place of occurrence to act as a witness and it took him around 30 Minutes
to 1 hr to reach the place of occurrence. He accepted the suggestion that before

law laid down by the Apex Court and consequently the trial Court proceedings
are vitiated, cannot be accepted. These arguments in view of the authoritative
finding laid down by the Apex Court in Mukesh Singh (Supra) is therefore
rejected.
28. The second argument of the counsel for the appellant that the secret
information received by the investigating agency was not reduced to writing on
the evidence available in this case also cannot be accepted. The evidence on
record reveals that this search and seizure was made during a random checking
of vehicles plying on a National Highways between Champhai and Zokhawthar
particularly at a place called Hringlangtlang Pend on the eve of the
Independence Day. The search was made at around 3.30 PM which is before
sunset. P.W.-1, the seizing officer, in his deposition stated that upon looking
inside the vehicle, he found no other passenger except the driver and the
present appellant. Looking at the driver, he found him nervous and he suspected
something was wrong. He requested the driver to switch off the engine and
open the bonnet. After the bonnet was opened, seizure of contraband articles
from a box/carton under the bonnet was recovered. In his deposition, he stated
that the recovery, seizure and repacking was done in the presence of the civilian
Page No.# 25/30
witnesses.
These arguments of the counsel for the appellant also cannot be accepted in
view of the fact that the evidence of the independent witnesses support the
prosecution case that the contraband articles were recovered from a box/carton
from under the bonnet of the Sumo vehicle which is driven by the accused No. 1
and in which the present appellant is also present.
29. As held in Mukesh Singh (Supra) by the Apex Court that the testimony of
police personnel will have to be treated in the same manner as any of the
witnesses. From the evidence, it is seen that the testimony of the seizing officer,
P.W-1, was not shaken during cross-examination. That apart, the independent
witnesses also support the testimony of the P.W.-1, the seizing officer. In that
view of the matter, this contention of the counsel for the appellant cannot be
accepted and the same is, therefore, rejected.
30. The arguments of the appellant that there is no evidence that the sample
articles were the articles examined by the FSL as there is no forwarding report
also cannot be accepted in view of the evidence available on record which
shows the seized items were produced before the Judicial Magistrate and in the
presence of Judicial Magistrate, the accused person and the independent
witnesses; four samples were taken out of the seized article and were
forwarded to the FSL report. This is also found to be recorded in the Judgment.
That apart, from the evidence adduced, it is seen that there is no dispute raised
by the appellant during trial regarding the correctness of the FSL report.
Consequently, the argument sought to be raised by the appellant cannot be
accepted in view of the fact that the sampling and weighing was conducted in
the presence of and independent witnesses as well as in the presence of
accused persons themselves before the Judicial Magistrate.
Page No.# 26/30
31. That apart, this Court in Crl. Appeal No. 21/2015 dated 03.03.2016 has
already held that FSL report may be relied upon in evidence without
examination of the chemical examiner. In this context, the apex Court has laid
down the law in Gangula Satyamurty, reported in AIR 1997 SC 1588.
32. In view of the law holding this field as noticed above, the arguments of
the appellant that the FSL report could not have been used in evidence without
examination of the chemical examiner namely P.W-4 is hereby rejected.
33. In so far as the arguments advanced on behalf of the appellant that the
appellant was not in conscious possession, this Court finds from the evidence
that an offer of Rs. 10,000/- was made for carrying and delivering of the goods
from Zokhawthar to Aizawl by the appellant and the other accused persons.
While it is true that there is no evidence to suggest that the contraband was put
in the carton/box by the accused persons or by some other persons in their
presence, however, the fact remains that the accused persons accepted the
delivery of the carton from Zokhawthar to Aizawl stated to contain some
medicines. If the accused persons believed that the box contained medicine,
there was no occasion for the accused persons to conceal the said box under
the bonnet of the vehicle near the engine block. At the time of the seizure,
there is evidence on record to show that there was no other passengers in the
vehicle except the accused persons. From the evidence available before the
learned Trial Court it is seen that at no stage the accused persons denied the
recovery of the contraband articles which was seized from the finding vehicle in
which only the accused persons were found. The consistent plea of the accused
persons was that it was not recovered from their conscious possession. Under
such circumstances, the accused persons have failed to explain as to why the
said box was required to be concealed near the engine block under the bonnet.
Page No.# 27/30
No explanation to that effect is seen in the statement made of the accused
during their examination under Section 313 CrPC. In view of all of the above,
the arguments of the learned counsel for the appellant that the appellant was
not in conscious possession cannot be accepted and is therefore rejected.
34. The contention of the learned counsel for the appellant is that the
independent witnesses did not support the recovery of the contraband seized
articles from the appellant also cannot be accepted as the same is contrary to
the evidence adduced before the Trial Court. The evidence of P.W.3, who was an
independent witness clearly reveals that the seized articles were recovered from
under the bonnet of the seized vehicle. Perusal of the evidence available on
record revealed that the evidence adduced in chief by the P.W.2 & 3 could not
be shaken during the cross-examination. As such, the evidence on record clearly
does not support the contention raised by the learned counsel for the appellant
and the same is therefore rejected. In view of the discussions made above, the
further contention of the appellant that independent witnesses did not support
the case of the prosecution also fails and is therefore rejected.
35. In so far as the third argument of the learned counsel for the appellant is
concerned that the contraband items were not recovered on the conscious
possession of the appellant. It is seen from the evidence adduced that the
seized contraband articles were recovered from under the Bonnet of the Sumo
vehicle which was inside a box/carton. Under the 313 examination of the
accused/appellant, no explanation was provided for as to how and why the
seized articles were kept in the bonnet of the vehicle when there are only two
persons travelling in the sumo vehicle without any other passenger. There is
also no evidence laid by the defence that the seized articles were never
recovered from the vehicle and/or were planned by the investigating agency.
Page No.# 28/30
Under such circumstances, the recovery of the seized contraband articles from
under the bonnet of the Sumo vehicle is not denied by the accused persons. It
is also seen that the FSL report never been questioned before the learned trial
Court. As such as has been held by the Apex Court in Gangula Satya Murthy
(Supra), the report relied upon by the Court without examination of the Officer
conducting the tests where no dispute was raised before the learned Trial Court
in respect of the said report, there is no infirmity in the trial Court accepting the
said report of the FSL where the results of the tests of the samples drawn from
the seized articles are found to be positive for heroin.
36. In Mohan Lal Vs. State of Punjab, reported in (2015) 6 SCC 222, the Apex
Court while examining an appeal under NDPS Act elaborately dealt with the
interpretation of the term “possession” under NDPS Act as well as with
reference to the Opium Act, 1878. The Apex Court held as under:
“The concept of possession is basically connected to “actus of physical control
and custody”. Attributing this meaning in the strict sense would be understanding
the factum of possession in a narrow sense. With the passage of time there has
been a gradual widening of the concept and the quintessential meaning of the
word “possession”. There is a degree of flexibility in the use of the said term and
that is why the word “possession” can be usefully defined and understood with
reference to the contextual purpose for the said expression. Over the years,
courts have refrained from adopting a doctrinaire approach towards defining
possession. A functional and flexible approach in defining and understanding the
possession as a concept is acceptable and thereby emphasis has been laid on
different possessory rights according to the commands and justice of the social
policy. Thus, the word “possession” in the context of any enactment would
depend upon the object and purpose of the enactment and an appropriate
meaning has to be assigned to the word to effectuate the said object. (Paras 11
and 15) The term “possession” ordinarily consists of two elements. First, it refers
Page No.# 29/30
to the corpus or the physical control and the second, it refers to the animus or
intent which has reference to exercise of the said control. Coming to the context
of Section 18 of the NDPS Act, it would have a reference to the concept of
conscious possession. The legislature while enacting the said law was absolutely
aware of the said element. The word “possession” refers to a mental state as is
noticeable from the language employed in Section 35 of the NDPS Act. It includes
knowledge of a fact. That apart, Section 35 raises a presumption as to knowledge
and culpable mental state from the possession of illicit articles. The expression
“possess or possessed” is often used in connection with statutory offences of
being in possession of prohibited drugs and contraband substances. Conscious or
mental state of possession is necessary and that is the reason for enacting
Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 1985.”
37. As such it has been held that the word “possession” refers to the mental
state as is noticeable from the language employed in Section 35 of the NDPS
Act. It includes knowledge of a fact. The evidence before the learned Trial Court
in the present appeal clearly reveal that the appellant along with his companion
who were driver/traveller in the Sumo did not offer any other explanation for
the recovery of the packets/carton from under the bonnet near the engine block
of the vehicle containing the seized contraband articles in their 313 statement.
There was no argument before the learned Trial Court denying the recovery
itself. The only argument was that it was not recovered from their conscious
possession. The evidence adduced before the learned Trial Court do not suggest
that a box was inserted inside the engine without the knowledge of the
appellant and his companion. As discussed above, the argument of the learned
counsel for the appellant that the contraband seized articles were not recovered
from their conscious possession fails and therefore cannot be accepted.
Page No.# 30/30
38. Upon due consideration of the evidences adduced before the Trial Court as
well as the law and the principles laid down by the Apex Court in the Judgments
discussed above, we find that the prosecution has prima facie established the
charge brought against the accuseds. However, the accused persons, including
the appellant herein had failed to discharge the burden to rebut the
presumption under Section 35 of the NDPS Act. From the evidence brought on
record, it has been established that the appellant, along with his companion,
had transported the seized contraband articles consciously and with knowledge.
The learned Special Judge, NDPS Act, Champhai, in our view, has correctly
appreciated the evidences on record while rendering the Judgment and Order
dated 15.12.2021 holding the appellant and the other accused persons guilty of
the offences charged with and had accordingly convicted them under Section
21(c)/25/29 of the NDPS Act and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for
a period of 12 years with fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees twenty-thousand) each
and in default of payment of fine, directed to further undergo Simple
Imprisonment for 2 (two) months each. We do not find any justifiable ground to
interfere with the findings and conclusions reached by the learned Trial Court.
39. In view of the above discussions, we find no merit in this appeal and the
same is accordingly dismissed.
40. Return the LCR.
JUDGE JUDGE
Comparing Assistant

judgments.case_name: Crl.Pet./3/2023 of Smt. Lalnunmawii Vs State of Mizoram r/b Secretary/Commissioner, Excise and Narcotics Department and Anr.
judgments.text:
Page No.# 1/7
GAHC030001682023
THE GAUHATI HIGH COURT
(HIGH COURT OF ASSAM, NAGALAND, MIZORAM AND ARUNACHAL PRADESH)
Case No. : Crl.Pet./3/2023
Smt. Lalnunmawii
Phunchawng Mel-6, Aizawl, Mizoram
VERSUS
State of Mizoram r/b Secretary/Commissioner, Excise and Narcotics Department and
Anr.
Aizawl2:The Officer-in-Charge
Anti Narcotics Squad
Commissionerate of Excise and Narcotic
Advocate for the Petitioner : Mr. J H Ramneihmawia
Advocate for the Respondent : P.P./Addl.PP, Mizoram
BEFORE
HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE NELSON SAILO
ORDER
Date : 20-04-2023
Heard Mr. J.H. Ramneihmawia, learned counsel for the petitioner, who
submits that the petitioner has filed the instant petition under Section 482 of
the Cr.P.C., praying for the release of her motor vehicle i.e., Maruti Suzuki Ciaz
Smart Hybrid Delta bearing Registration No. MZ 01 T 5265, which was seized by
the Excise & Narcotics Personnel on 29.12.2022 because of the alleged recovery
of 1.885 kilograms of Methamphetamine from the possession of the accused
persons using the vehicle at Tuikhurhlu, Seling, Aizawl District, Mizoram. Due to
Page No.# 2/7
the recovery of the alleged drugs, Excise Case No. N-217/2022 dated
30.12.2022 was registered against the accused persons. Upon completion of the
investigation, the Excise & Narcotics Department has filed the charge sheet No.
Ex-(ANS) 15/2023 dated 30.01.2023 against 4 (four) accused persons. The
accused No. 1 is the elder brother of the instant petitioner.
2. The learned counsel submits that the petitioner is the registered owner of
the vehicle and she has no involvement and no knowledge about the carrying of
the alleged drugs in the said vehicle. He submits that since the seizure of the
said vehicle on 29.12.2022, the vehicle is in the custody of the Excise &
Narcotics Department and is being kept in the open. As such, the vehicle is
being subjected to rust and decay and if the same is not released to the
petitioner pending disposal of the trial, the petitioner is bound to suffer
irreparable loss and hardship. He therefore submits that the same may be
released to the petitioner and that the petitioner is ready to give any
undertaking as may be required for release of the said vehicle.
3. Ms. Mary L. Khiangte, learned Additional Public Prosecutor, on the other
hand submits that the petitioner has only annexed some documents of the
vehicle obtained through Vahan app. and therefore, it cannot be said for sure
that the petitioner is the registered owner of the vehicle without seeing the
original documents. She further submits that since the accused No. 1 is the
elder brother of the petitioner, it is unbelievable that the petitioner was not
aware about the use of the vehicle for carrying the alleged drugs. She submits
that the vehicle otherwise is liable to be confiscated in terms of the relevant
provisions of the ND&PS Act.
4. I have heard the submissions made by the learned counsels for the rival
Page No.# 3/7
parties and I have perused the materials available on record.
5. The case of the prosecution is that the alleged drugs have been recovered
from the accused persons, who were travelling in the said vehicle. As a result,
while arresting the accused persons and seizing the alleged drugs, the vehicle
has also been seized by the Excise & Narcotics Department and since December,
2022, the same appears to be left in the open as can be seen from the
photograph annexed by the petitioner in the criminal petition as Annexure-10.
Although the charge sheet has been filed and trial has commenced admittedly
but it is not known as to when the same can be concluded. The prosecution has
also cited as many as 8 (eight) prosecution witnesses and as submitted at the
bar today, the evidence of the prosecution witness No. 1 is yet to be recorded.
6. The petitioner before coming to this Court had filed Criminal Misc. Appln.
No. 8/2023 before the learned Judge, Special Court, ND&PS Act, Aizawl praying
for release of the said vehicle but however, the application was rejected by the
learned Judge.
7. The Apex Court in Sunderbhai Ambalal Desai (supra) appreciated the
purpose and import of Section 451 Cr.PC. In doing so, the Apex Court had also
referred to its earlier decision in Basavva Kom Dyamangouda Patil (supra).
Paragraph Nos. 5, 7, 8, 15, 17 & 18 of Sunderbhai Ambalal Desai (supra) may
be gainfully abstracted below:-
“5. Section 451 clearly empowers the court to pass appropriate orders with regard to
such property, such as:
(1) for the proper custody pending conclusion of the inquiry or trial;
(2) to order it to be sold or otherwise disposed of, after recording such evidence as it
thinks necessary;
(3) if the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, to dispose of the same.
Page No.# 4/7
7. In our view, the powers under Section 451 CrPC should be exercised expeditiously
and judiciously. It would serve various purposes, namely:
1. owner of the article would not suffer because of its remaining unused or by its
misappropriation;
2. court or the police would not be required to keep the article in safe custody;
3. if the proper panchnama before handing over possession of the article is prepared,
that can be used in evidence instead of its production before the court during the trial.
If necessary, evidence could also be recorded describing the nature of the property in
detail; and
4. this jurisdiction of the court to record evidence should be exercised promptly so
that there may not be further chance of tampering with the articles.
8. The question of proper custody of the seized article is raised in a number of
matters. In Basavva Kom Dyamangouda Patil v. State of Mysore this Court dealt with a
case where the seized articles were not available for being returned to the
complainant. In that case, the recovered ornaments were kept in a trunk in the police
station and later it was found missing, the question was with regard to payment of
those articles. In that context, the Court observed as under:
“4. The object and scheme of the various provisions of the Code appear to be that
where the property which has been the subject-matter of an offence is seized by the
police it ought not to be retained in the custody of the court or of the police for any
time longer than what is absolutely necessary. As the seizure of the property by the
police amounts to a clear entrustment of the property to a government servant, the
idea is that the property should be restored to the original owner after the necessity
to retain it ceases. It is manifest that there may be two stages when the property may
be returned to the owner. In the first place it may be returned during any inquiry or
trial. This may particularly be necessary where the property concerned is subject to
speedy or natural decay. There may be other compelling reasons also which may
justify the disposal of the property to the owner or otherwise in the interest of justice.
The High Court and the Sessions Judge proceeded on the footing that one of the
essential requirements of the Code is that the articles concerned must be produced
before the court or should be in its custody. The object of the Code seems to be that
any property which is in the c control of the court either directly or indirectly should
Page No.# 5/7
be disposed of by the court and a just and proper order should be passed by the court
regarding its disposal. In a criminal case, the police always acts under the direct
control of the court and has to take orders from it at every stage of an inquiry or trial.
In this broad sense, therefore, the court exercises an overall control on the actions of
the police officers in every case where it has taken cognizance."
9. ………….
10. ………….
11. …………
12. …………
13. …………
14 ………..
15. Learned Senior Counsel Mr. Dholakia, appearing for the State of Gujarat further
submitted that at present in the police station premises, a number of vehicles are kept
unattended and vehicles become junk day by day. It is his contention that appropriate
directions should be given to the Magistrates who are dealing with such questions to
hand over such vehicles to their owners or to the person from whom the said vehicles
are seized by taking appropriate bond and guarantee for the return of the said
vehicles if required by the court at any point of time.
16. …………..
17. Whatever be the situation, it is of no use to keep such seized vehicles at the police
stations for a long period. It is for the Magistrate to pass appropriate orders
immediately by taking appropriate bond and guarantee as well as security for return
of the said vehicles, if required at any point of time. This can be done pending hearing
of applications for return of such vehicles.
18. In case where the vehicle is not claimed by the accused, owner, or the insurance
company or by a third person, then such vehicle may be ordered to be auctioned by
the court. If the said vehicle is insured with the insurance company then the insurance
company be informed by the court to take possession of the vehicle which is not
claimed by the owner or a third person. If the insurance company fails to take
Page No.# 6/7
possession, the vehicles may be sold as per the direction of the court. The court
would pass such order within a period of six months from the date of production of
the said vehicle before the court. In any case, before handing over possession of such
vehicles, appropriate photographs of the said vehicle should be taken and detailed
panchnama should be prepared.”
8. From the above abstract, it may be seen that according to the Apex Court,
Section 451 Cr.PC empowers the Court to pass appropriate orders with regard to
property including vehicles for the proper custody pending conclusion of the
inquiry or trial. The Apex Court in the given facts of that case observed that
whatever situation it may be, it would be of no use to keep a seized vehicles at
the Police Station for a long period and it would be for the Magistrate concerned
to pass appropriate orders immediately by taking appropriate bond, guarantee
as well as security for return of the said vehicle, as and when required by the
Court and at any point of time. In fact, before handing over the possession of
such vehicles, appropriate photographs of the vehicle should be taken and
detailed panchnama should be prepared.
9. Thus, upon having considered the projection made by the petitioner as well
as the State respondents and importantly the decision of the Apex Court, I am
of the considered view that the learned Trial Court ought to have considered
release of the said vehicle by following the safeguards as observed by the Apex
Court in the aforesaid referred case. In view of above, pending conclusion of the
trial, the vehicle is directed to be released to the petitioner, however, only after
the safeguards as provided herein above has been secured. The petitioner shall
appear before the learned Trial Court along with the certified copy of this order
on 27.04.2023 and on her appearance, the learned Trial Court shall cause the
preparation of all the safeguards as spelt out in the case of Sunderbhai Ambalal
Page No.# 7/7
Desai (supra) and thereafter, release the vehicle to the petitioner.
10. With the above observation and direction, the Criminal Petition stands
disposed of.
JUDGE
Comparing Assistant

judgments.case_name: Crl.Pet./1/2022 of Beikrystkypacha Hlychho and Anr. Vs State of Mizoram  and 5 Ors.
bench: HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE ARUN DEV CHOUDHURY
judgments.text:
Page No.# 1/7
GAHC030000462022
THE GAUHATI HIGH COURT
(HIGH COURT OF ASSAM, NAGALAND, MIZORAM AND ARUNACHAL PRADESH)
Case No. : Crl.Pet./1/2022
Beikrystkypacha Hlychho and Anr.
S/o Chholai Hlychho
R/o New Colony I,Saiha, Mizoram 2: Lalduhsaki Khawlhring
New Colony I
Saiha
Mizora
VERSUS
State of Mizoram and 5 Ors.
Aizawl, Mizoram
Advocate for the Petitioner : Mr. T Lalnunsiama
Advocate for the Respondent : Mr C Zoramchhana (P.P., Mizoram) for R1 - R5
- B e f o r e-
Hon’ble Mr. Justice arun dev choudhury
29.09.2023
1. Heard Mr. T. Lainunsiama, learned counsel for the petitioners. Also
heard Mr. C. Zoramchhana, learned Public Prosecutor for the State of
Mizoram. Also heard Mr. J. C. Lalnunsanga, learned counsel for the
respondent No. 6/informant.
Page No.# 2/7
2. The present application is filed under section 482 Cr.P.C., 1973 for
setting aside and quashing an FIR filed by the respondent No. 6, which was
registered as Aizawl PS Case No.491/2021 under sections 406/420 IPC
1860 against the petitioners.
3. The principle of exercise of power under section 482Cr.P.C. to quash FIR
and charge sheet on the basis of different pronouncement of the hon’ble
apex court can be summarized in the following manner.
I. When the allegations made in the FIR or in a complaint is taken
at their face value and accepted, it does not prima facie constitute
any offence or do not make out a case against the accused. The
court is to see that if the complaint/FIR is taken at their face value,
no cognizable offence is made out.
II. Such power can also be exercised when the facts narrated are
absurd and inherently improbable, or manifestly attended with
malafide or with an ulterior motive.
III. However, while exercising its power the court is not to embark
upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness of the allegation
made in the FIR/complaint.
IV. It is also well settled that such power is to be sparingly
exercised and in exceptional cases, so as to avoid miscarriage of
justice and also in a situation where there is abuse of process of the
court.
V. The power under section 482 Cr.P.C being wide that while
Page No.# 3/7
exercising such extra ordinary power the court must be cautious and
need to be very diligent.
4. Now let this court consider the factum of the present challenge
based on the aforesaid principles of the law. For proper appreciation of
the issue in hand the FIR is quoted herein below:
“To,
The Officer In-charge,
Aizawl Police Station,
Aizawl, Mizoram
Sub – First Information Report.
Sir,
Around November 2019 Beikristakypacha Hlychho, New Colony-I, Siaha
said that he acquired a work at Gamon India NH-54 Package-2 from Khumtung
to Keitum and I invest a sum of Rs. 74,00,000/- (seventy four lakhs). I was
told to transfer the said money to M/s Zeliezhu & Sons from Mizoram Rural
Bank Chandmari Branch in the name of Khawlhring Agency, Proprietor
Lalduhsaki, Lawngtlai, L-3. The owner of Khawlhring Agency Lalduhsaki is the
wife of Beikristakypacha Hlychoo. However he did not get the said work and
he told us that the money given to Khawlhring Agency is “You have deposited
it, we are going to have another contract”. Mr. Beikristakypacha Hlychho
established Andrea Enterprise and that Andrea Enterprise got a work order
from Bhartia Infra Projects Ltd on 22.7.2020 for widening & upgradation 2
lane, Aizawl- Tuipang.
Then he let me work in this contract work. I completed road making work
on May, 2021. I know that BIPL has released the bill, however,
Beikristakypacha Hlychho refused to pay me the said bill. That the total
amount of my money along with the amount deposited previously to
Page No.# 4/7
Khawlhring Agency Rs. 74,00,000/- (seventy four lakhs) and my working bill
under BIPL amounting Rs. 142,00,000/- (one hundred and forty two lakhs)
making the full amount to Rs. 200,00,016/- (Two hundred lakhs and sixteen). I
made several request to pay me the said sum of money, however, he made
several excuse and did not pay me till now. I therefore, request you to take
actions so that I can get my money and take actions according to law for
cheating me.
Sincerely Yours
(Sd/ (ZIRSANGPUII)
W/O Zothanpuia
R/o Seling, Champhai Road”
5. From the aforesaid FIR the following facts can be ascertained
I. That there was an agreement between the informant and
the accused for execution of some contract
II. In terms of the said contract the accused are required to
pay some money to the informant.
III. It is the further case as reflected in the FIR that the FIR
has been lodged for the reason that after trying her level best, the
informant has failed to get her money back, then she completed
the work in terms of their agreement.
6. Section 405 IPC defines the criminal breach of trust. A reading of the
aforesaid provision of law, the essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust
can be summarized as below:
A. There must be an entrustment of property or dominion over it upon
Page No.# 5/7
the accused.
B. The accused upon whom such property is entrusted has dishonestly
used or disposed of the property in violation of any provision of
law which prescribed the mode in which such trust is to be
discharged or of any contract made defining the discharge of
such trust.
7. In the case of R K Dalmia Vs Delhi Administration reported in 1963 1
SCR 253, the Hon’ble Apex Court held that the definition as given under
Section 405 Cr.P.C. does not restrict the property to be movable or immovable
one and the property used in the Cr.P.C. is having a much wider sense than
expression movable property. Accordingly, the Hon’ble Apex Court in RK
Dalmia (supra) concluded that there is no good reason to restrict the
meaning of word ‘property’ to movable property only when it is used without
any qualification under Section 405 IPC.
8. Section 415 IPC defines cheating. The essential ingredients of cheating are
deception of any person, fraudulent and dishonest inducement with intent
to deliver any property or to have consent to retain any property and also
an intention whereby an inducement is made to a person to do or omit to
do anything which he would not or omit if he was so deceived.
9. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Hriday Ranjan Prasad Verma Vs.
State of Bihar and Anr. reported in 2000 4 SCC 168 clarified that there
is a very fine line while making a distinction between mere breach of
contract and cheating, which is criminal one and breach of contract. Law is
by now well settled that breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal
Page No.# 6/7
prosecution of cheating until and unless the fraudulent or dishonest
intention of cheating is made out in the complaint itself.
10. From the allegations made in the FIR, in the considered opinion of this court
even the allegation are taken at their face value and accepted in entirety,
do not make out any prima facie case to constitute an offence under
section 406/420 IPC rather the matter is totally civil in nature and it is
nothing but a claim of money due arising out of contract for execution of
work between the informant and the accused and relates to contractual
liability and payment of due arising out of such contract and breach of
terms of contract. Further, this court is unable to find out any
statement/averment or whisper, which shows that the accused was having
an initial deception in mind to cheat the informant at the stage of entering
into the contract/agreement.
11. This Court also perused the case diary produced which reflects that there is
no material available on record and / or collected by the Investigating
Authority to proceed against the petitioners for commission of the offence
under Section 406/420 of IPC. What the Investigating Authority did is first,
arrested the accused persons, secondly, seized their bank accounts and
started enquiry about their entitlement of the bill for execution of the
contract by them. The Investigating Authority has not been able to collect
any materials even to remotely indicate that there was some entrustment
of property or dominion over it upon the accused persons and that the
accused persons have dishonestly used or disposed of such property
entrusted upon them in violation of any provision of law.
12. There is also no material in the case diary to suggest any initial deception,
Page No.# 7/7
fraudulent and dishonest and inducement on the part of the accused
persons rather from the material collected, it is clear that the case is
nothing but a breach of contract.
13. Therefore, in view of the aforesaid, this court finds that no case under
Section 406/420/ IPC is made out on a bare reading of the FIR as well as
the materials so far collected by the Investigating Authority.
14. In view of the aforesaid the present petition stands allowed by setting aside
and quashing the FIR which was registered as Aizawl PS Case No.491/2021
under sections 406/420 IPC 1860.
15. While parting with the record, it is made clear that quashing of the FIR shall
not debar the informant for recovery of money, if any, by following due
process available under law.
JUDGE
Comparing Assistant
